Keywords: Bog Myrtle and Yarrow Gruit Blend
RagShortTexts: Archbishops monopolized herbal gruit mixtures, challenged by hopped beer allowing long.

Variants.Content: Northern European brewing underwent a commercial transformation. Historically, ale was flavored and preserved using 'gruit'—a secret herbal concoction of bog myrtle, yarrow, and wild rosemary monopolized by prince-archbishops (gruitrecht). The adoption of cultivated hops introduced antibacterial bittering agents that preserved cask beer for months, unlocking long-distance export across Baltic sea lanes.

Ecclesiastical magnates resisted hops to protect lucrative gruit monopolies, but autonomous Hanseatic cities embraced hopped brewing, making beer casks primary ballast cargo for northern shipping fleets.
Gruit ale sours into vinegar in days. Hopped brews taste pleasantly bitter and remain clear in cellars throughout winter, shielding tavern goers from tainted ditch water.
